individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper proposes FM4NPP, a foundation model for experimental particle physics using sparse detector data from the sPHENIX Time Projection Chamber. The authors introduce a large simulated dataset (11M+ pp collision events), a Hierarchical Raster Scan method to serialize unordered 3D spacepoints into sequences, and a self-supervised objective based on k-Next-Nearest-Neighbor prediction with event-difficulty rescaling. The model uses a Mamba2 backbone and is scaled up to 188M parameters. Frozen FM features are combined with lightweight adapters for three downstream tasks: track finding, particle identification, and noise tagging. Experiments show scaling laws, improved downstream performance over baselines, data-efficient adaptation, and task-agnostic representations that become separable after a linear projection.
Strengths: First demonstration of a scalable foundation model for sparse particle detector data, with a novel serialization and self-supervised objective.
Comprehensive scaling study across model size, dataset size, and compute, using a new open dataset.
Strong downstream performance with frozen FM and lightweight adapters, including outperforming the official sPHENIX reconstruction pipeline on a restricted track sample.
The hierarchical raster scan and k-Next-Nearest-Neighbor prediction are well motivated and described in detail.
Data-efficient adaptation analysis clearly shows benefits of pretraining, especially with limited labeled data.
Weaknesses: The claim that the FM consistently outperforms all baselines is not fully supported: for noise tagging, OneFormer3D achieves higher macro recall (0.9404 vs 0.9367) though lower accuracy.
No statistical uncertainties or significance tests are reported for any downstream metric.

The abstract and text claim representations can be specialized via a 'single linear mapping', but the downstream adapters include self-attention/transformer layers; only the visualization uses a linear probe.
No ablation study on the serialization strategy or the choice of k in the pretraining objective; sensitivity to these design choices is unknown.
Data scaling is only shown for the m3 model; whether larger models follow the same power law is not demonstrated.
Baseline models may not be optimally tuned; hyperparameter search details for Exa.TrkX and EggNet adaptations are sparse.
Questions: How were the baseline models tuned, and were their hyperparameters optimized to a similar degree as the proposed adapters?
What is the effect of the hierarchical raster scan compared to naive serializations (e.g., Hilbert curve or radial sort) on pretraining loss and downstream performance?
How does the choice of k in k-Next-Nearest-Neighbor affect downstream task performance?
Are the reported metric differences statistically significant given the test set size?
Does the FM pretrained on simulated data transfer to real detector data, or is there a domain gap?
Why is noise tagging recall lower than OneFormer3D, and can the loss re-weighting or adapter be modified to improve it?
Limitations: The model is evaluated only on simulated p+p collisions at 200 GeV; real detector effects, calibration, and other collision systems (e.g., heavy ions) are not addressed.
Only TPC spacepoints are used; calorimeter and silicon tracker information is excluded, limiting the scope of downstream tasks.
The largest model requires substantial compute (64 H100 GPUs for 72 hours), which may limit reproducibility.
The pretraining objective and serialization are tailored to this detector geometry; generalizing to other detectors may require redesign.
Downstream tasks are all point-level segmentation; the FM's utility for other tasks (e.g., generation or regression) is unexplored.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper introduces FM4NPP, a foundation model for experimental particle physics detector data. It contributes a simulated sPHENIX TPC dataset of more than 11 million collision events, three downstream tasks (track finding, particle identification, noise tagging), and a self-supervised training method based on hierarchical raster-scan serialization and k-next-nearest-neighbor prediction. The model uses Mamba2 backbones up to 188M parameters, and the authors demonstrate neural scaling behavior, data-efficient adaptation, and improved performance over several baselines when the frozen pretrained model is paired with lightweight adapters. Additional analyses suggest that the learned representations are task-agnostic and become separable after a single linear projection.
Strengths: Addresses an important and timely question: whether foundation-model-style pretraining can work for sparse, non-language scientific data such as particle detector spacepoints.
Releases a large, realistic simulated dataset with multiple downstream physics tasks, which is a valuable resource for the community.
Proposes a concrete serialization scheme and a self-supervised objective tailored to the geometry of TPC data, going beyond naive next-token prediction.
Systematically studies scaling with model size, dataset size, and compute, using mu-parameterization for hyperparameter transfer.

The frozen-FM + lightweight-adapter pipeline outperforms adapter-only and several GNN baselines, especially in low-label regimes, and PCA/t-SNE analyses support the task-agnostic representation claim.
Weaknesses: The k-next-nearest-neighbor objective may not be causal under the hierarchical raster scan: boxes are ordered by center coordinates and not strictly by radius, so a query point's larger-radius neighbors can potentially appear earlier in the serialized sequence, causing information leakage; the paper does not demonstrate that all target neighbors are future tokens.

Main Table 2 and Appendix Tables 3 and 4 report inconsistent metrics for FM4NPP(m6) on particle identification and noise tagging; for example, PID accuracy is 0.9039 in the main table but 0.8547 in the appendix, and noise-tagging accuracy is 0.9713 versus 0.9662, with no explanation.
Scaling-law claims are based on single runs without error bars, fitted exponents, or a compute-optimal analysis; the plateau at m6 is noted but not investigated.

The baselines may be handicapped: Exa.TrkX and EggNet are adapted with reduced features and manually tuned thresholds, and OneFormer3D is used with default S3DIS settings, so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is not fully established.
The comparison to the official sPHENIX reconstruction pipeline is restricted to high-transverse-momentum, long tracks, which is a favorable subset; no overall comparison is provided.
The paper has no explicit limitations section and lacks clear public-release instructions for code, checkpoints, or dataset access, making reproducibility incomplete.
Questions: Is the proposed k-next-nearest-neighbor prediction strictly causal? Please verify that for every query spacepoint, all k target neighbors with larger radius appear later in the serialized sequence; if not, what prevents the model from copying previously seen coordinates?
Why do the main text and appendix report different numbers for FM4NPP(m6) on PID and noise tagging? Which set of results is correct?
What are the fitted power-law exponents and confidence intervals for the scaling curves in Figure 5, and how many random seeds were used?
How were the number of track queries, transformer decoder layers, and loss weights chosen for the track-finding adapter, and how sensitive are the results to these hyperparameters?
What are the exact train/validation/test splits and the number of labeled events used in each downstream task?
Were ablations performed on the serialization strategy (e.g., random, Hilbert, radial, vs. hierarchical raster scan) and on event-difficulty rescaling? What were the quantitative results?
What thresholds and track-selection criteria were used for the official sPHENIX pipeline comparison, and what is the performance on the full track sample?
Is the dataset, code, and pretrained model publicly available, and under what license?
Limitations: The pretraining objective may suffer from information leakage due to the lack of strict radial ordering in the serialization, which could inflate the reported performance.
Results are limited to simulated p+p collisions at the sPHENIX TPC; generalization to heavy-ion collisions, other detector geometries, and real data is untested.
No error bars or seed variability are reported, and the scaling study is based on a modest number of model sizes.
Baseline models are adapted with manual thresholds and reduced input features, which may not reflect their full capability.
The main text and appendix contain inconsistent results for the same model and tasks, reducing confidence in the reported numbers.
The paper does not provide an explicit discussion of computational cost in FLOPs or energy consumption, nor a dedicated limitations section.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes FM4NPP, a foundation model for sparse particle detector data from the sPHENIX TPC. It introduces a dataset of more than 11 million simulated p+p collision events, a hierarchical raster scan serialization method, and a k-next-nearest-neighbor self-supervised objective for Mamba2. The pretrained model is frozen and paired with lightweight task-specific adapters for track finding, particle identification, and noise tagging. The paper reports neural scaling behavior up to 188M parameters and claims consistent performance gains over baselines on all three downstream tasks.
Strengths: Large-scale realistic simulated dataset with 11M+ events and three downstream tasks, which is a valuable resource for the particle physics ML community.
Novel combination of hierarchical raster scan serialization and k-next-nearest-neighbor self-supervised prediction is tailored to sparse, geometry-rich detector data.
Demonstrates scaling behavior across model size, dataset size, and compute, and shows data-efficient adaptation with frozen representations.
Frozen FM plus lightweight adapters outperforms specialized baselines on track finding, PID, and noise tagging, with particularly strong gains on track finding.
Weaknesses: Major numerical inconsistencies: Table 2 reports FM4NPP(m6) PID accuracy 0.9039, recall 0.7652, precision 0.8782 and noise tagging accuracy 0.9713, recall 0.9367, precision 0.9190, while Appendix Tables 3 and 4 report different values (e.g., PID accuracy 0.8547, noise tagging accuracy 0.9662). This undermines reproducibility and confidence in the reported results.
The paper does not explicitly state whether downstream evaluation events are disjoint from the pretraining dataset, raising the risk of data contamination and inflating downstream performance.

The claim that FM representations are task-agnostic and can be specialized via a single linear mapping is supported only by qualitative PCA/t-SNE visualizations, not by quantitative linear probing or ablations.

Scaling-law claims are based on plots without fitted exponents, confidence intervals, or statistical error bars; the compute-scaling experiment confounds model size and training iterations, making the conclusions less rigorous.
Data-efficiency evidence is limited to the track-finding task; the abstract and introduction imply broader robust data-efficient adaptation without corresponding results for PID and noise tagging.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair: Exa.TrkX and EggNet were adapted without cell features and with thresholds chosen in an ad hoc manner, and no evidence of comparable hyperparameter tuning budget is provided.

The evaluation is entirely on simulated data from a single detector (sPHENIX TPC) and a single collision system (p+p at 200 GeV), so generalization to real data, heavy-ion collisions, or other detectors is untested.
Questions: Are the pretraining and downstream evaluation datasets disjoint? What is the exact split and are any downstream test events used during pretraining?
Which set of numbers is correct for FM4NPP on PID and noise tagging, those in Table 2 or those in Appendix Tables 3 and 4? Why do they differ?
How were the scaling-law exponents in Figure 5 estimated? Can you provide fitted power-law parameters and confidence intervals?

Was the hierarchical raster scan compared against alternative serializations (e.g., Hilbert curve, radial sort, random order) and was the k-next-nearest-neighbor objective compared to other pretext tasks?
Can you provide quantitative linear-probe results (e.g., linear classifier accuracy on frozen FM embeddings) for all three downstream tasks, rather than only PCA/t-SNE visualizations?
What is the inference-time computational cost and wall-clock latency of the full frozen 188M-parameter backbone plus adapter, compared to the GNN baselines?
How were hyperparameters for the baseline models chosen? Were they tuned with a comparable compute budget to the FM adapters?
Have any experiments been performed on real sPHENIX data, or is the model validated only on simulation? What domain-gap issues are anticipated?
Limitations: All results are on simulated data; transferability to real detector data is not demonstrated.
The model is developed and evaluated for the sPHENIX TPC in p+p collisions only; applicability to heavy-ion collisions or other detectors is unknown.
The noise-tagging definition relies on a kinematic threshold (momentum below 60 MeV/c) and may not match physics-analysis definitions in all contexts.
Pretraining the largest model requires 64 H100 GPUs for 72 hours, which may limit reproducibility and accessibility for many research groups.
The paper does not provide error bars or statistical significance tests for downstream metrics, making it difficult to judge whether performance differences are meaningful.
Some downstream classes have very low per-class recall (e.g., kaons in Table 4), which is obscured by macro-averaged metrics.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces FM4NPP, a foundation model for experimental particle physics built from simulated sPHENIX TPC detector data. It contributes a large-scale dataset (11M+ p+p collision events) with three downstream tasks (track finding, particle identification, noise tagging), a self-supervised pretraining method based on hierarchical raster scan serialization and k-next-nearest-neighbor prediction with a Mamba2 backbone, and scaling studies up to 188M parameters. Frozen FM features with lightweight adapters outperform several baselines across all tasks, and the paper analyzes data efficiency and representation structure.
Strengths: Provides a large-scale open dataset and benchmark for foundation-model research on sparse TPC data, which is a valuable resource for the NPP community.
Demonstrates clear neural scaling laws (power-law validation loss vs model size, data size, and compute) for detector data, a first for this domain.
Frozen pretrained features consistently outperform task-specific baselines (GNNs, OneFormer3D) with far fewer trainable parameters, and show strong data-efficiency gains with limited labels.
The representation analysis (PCA/t-SNE) gives qualitative evidence that a single linear projection can specialize FM embeddings, supporting the task-agnosticity claim.
The self-supervised objective and event-difficulty rescaling are well-motivated for sparse, spatially distributed detector data.
Weaknesses: Novelty is largely an application of existing techniques (Mamba2, NeRF positional encoding, set-prediction adapters, μP) to a new domain; the pretraining objective is a geometric prediction task closely aligned with the downstream tasks, so the demonstrated generalization is less surprising.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair: AdapterOnly on raw features is a weak baseline, and a stronger supervised baseline (e.g., a Mamba model trained end-to-end on each task) is missing; Exa.TrkX/EggNet adaptations are non-trivial and may not be optimally tuned.

No error bars or statistical significance are reported, and there are inconsistencies between main-table and appendix results (e.g., FM4NPP(m6) PID accuracy is 0.9039 in Table 2 but 0.8547 in Appendix Table 4), which undermines confidence.
The comparison with the official sPHENIX reconstruction pipeline is limited to high-pT tracks with ≥20 hits, which may not reflect overall tracking performance; a full-detector comparison is absent.

The claim that representations are task-agnostic is weakened because the pretraining objective uses radius-ordered neighbor prediction that directly encodes track-finding-relevant geometry; the observed separability hierarchy (track finding > PID > noise tagging) tracks task relevance.

No ablations are provided for the serialization strategy or the pretraining objective, so the benefit of the specific design choices over simpler alternatives (e.g., random order, Hilbert curve, masked prediction) is not isolated.
Questions: How does the FM compare to a Mamba2 model trained end-to-end (without pretraining) on each downstream task using the same adapter, with comparable compute?
What is the sensitivity of downstream performance to the hierarchical raster scan grid hyperparameters and to the choice of k in k-next-nearest-neighbor?
What is the breakdown of tracking efficiency/purity by track pT and η, especially for low-pT tracks?
Can a simple model on handcrafted features (energy, radius, position) achieve comparable PID/noise-tagging performance, and how does that inform the value of pretraining?
Are the main results reproducible given the discrepancies between the main text and appendix tables?
What is the computational cost for adapter training and inference, and how does the 188M FM compare to a smaller model under equal total compute budgets on downstream tasks?
Limitations: The dataset is entirely simulated; real detector data may have different noise and distortion characteristics not captured in the simulation.
The FM is pretrained and evaluated only on p+p collisions at 200 GeV; generalization to heavy-ion collisions or other collider geometries is untested.

All downstream tasks are point-level classification/segmentation; the paper does not demonstrate other task types (regression, generation, anomaly detection) that might be relevant to a foundation model.
The model uses only TPC data and does not incorporate other detector subsystems, limiting its scope as a general NPP foundation model.
Pretraining requires large compute (up to 72 H100-hours for the 188M model), and the paper does not provide a practical cost-performance recipe for resource-constrained groups.

review.Summary: The paper introduces FM4NPP, a foundation model for experimental particle physics detector data, trained self-supervised on more than 11 million simulated sPHENIX TPC collision events. It proposes a hierarchical raster scan serialization for sparse spacepoints, a Mamba2-based backbone, and a k-next-nearest-neighbor prediction objective with event-difficulty loss rescaling. The authors study scaling behavior up to 188M parameters, then evaluate frozen-FM-plus-lightweight-adapter models on track finding, particle identification, and noise tagging, reporting consistent improvements over adapted GNN and point-cloud baselines and evidence of data-efficient, task-agnostic representations.
Strengths: The construction of a large-scale (11M+ event) simulated dataset with realistic Geant4/sPHENIX simulation and three labeled downstream tasks is a potentially valuable community resource.
The hierarchical raster scan serialization and k-next-nearest-neighbor objective are thoughtful, physics-aware designs that address the unique sparsity and structure of detector data.
The paper provides a systematic scaling study across model size, dataset size, and compute, and applies μP-SSM for hyperparameter transfer, which is a useful contribution for scientific FMs.
Frozen-FM plus lightweight adapters outperform strong adapted baselines on track finding, PID, and noise tagging, and the data-efficiency experiments show clear gains in low-label regimes.
Embedding analyses (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP) support the claim that the pretrained features become linearly separable after a simple projection, offering insight into representation quality.
Weaknesses: There are major numerical inconsistencies between the main text and appendix: Table 2 reports PID accuracy 0.9039, recall 0.7652 and noise-tagging accuracy 0.9713, recall 0.9367 for FM4NPP(m6), while Appendix Tables 3 and 4 report 0.8547/0.6623 and 0.9662/0.9122 for the same model; this undermines confidence in the reported results.
No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are provided, so it is unclear whether observed FM gains over OneFormer3D and adapted baselines are statistically significant.

The pretraining objective and serialization choices are not ablated (e.g., k value, binning granularity, alternative objectives like masked autoencoding or contrastive learning), so the source of the FM's downstream benefit is not isolated.

All experiments use simulated data from a single detector (sPHENIX TPC); no validation on real data or other detector geometries is performed, so the claim of a generalizable particle-physics foundation model is not fully supported.
The 'open benchmark' claim is unsubstantiated: no dataset URL, license, or release instructions are provided, and no code is supplied, making the work difficult to reproduce.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair: Exa.TrkX and EggNet are adapted to sPHENIX without full original feature richness, OneFormer3D is used with S3DIS hyperparameters, and no compute/tuning budget comparison is reported.
The comparison against the official sPHENIX reconstruction pipeline is restricted to tracks with at least 20 spacepoints, pT > 1 GeV, and |eta| < 1.1; full-acceptance performance is not demonstrated.
Questions: What explains the discrepancy between main-text Table 2 and Appendix Tables 3-4 for FM4NPP(m6) PID and noise-tagging metrics? Which numbers are the final results?
Were all downstream experiments run with multiple seeds, and are the reported differences statistically significant? Please provide standard deviations or confidence intervals.
What are the exact train/validation/test splits, number of labeled events per downstream task, and dataset release URL/license?
How were adapter hyperparameters selected for FM4NPP versus the baselines, and is the comparison controlled for training compute or tuning budget?
Are there ablations for the pretraining objective (e.g., different k values, loss re-weighting, alternative self-supervised tasks) and for the serialization binning choices?
Has the FM been evaluated on real sPHENIX data or on other detector geometries to demonstrate generalizability beyond this simulation setup?
Limitations: All results are based on simulated data; real-data performance and sim-to-real transfer remain untested.
The model and dataset are not released in the paper, limiting reproducibility.
Evaluation is limited to one detector geometry (TPC spacepoints); extension to calorimeters, silicon trackers, or heavy-ion collisions is left as future work.
Inconsistencies between main and appendix tables suggest possible versioning or reporting errors; a corrected consolidated result table is needed.
The computational cost and environmental impact of training 188M-parameter models on 64 GPUs are not discussed.

meta_review_model.label: area_chair_meta_review

review.Summary: The paper introduces FM4NPP, a foundation model for sparse particle detector data from the sPHENIX Time Projection Chamber. It contributes a large simulated dataset of 11M+ proton-proton collision events, a hierarchical raster scan serialization method, a self-supervised k-next-nearest-neighbor prediction objective, and a Mamba2-based architecture scaled to 188M parameters. Frozen FM features with lightweight adapters are evaluated on track finding, particle identification, and noise tagging, with claims of improved performance over baselines, neural scaling behavior, and data-efficient task-agnostic representations. The reviewers are split: two recommend acceptance, citing the valuable dataset and promising approach, while three recommend rejection due to major numerical inconsistencies, insufficient ablations, lack of statistical rigor, and concerns about baseline fairness and reproducibility.
Strengths: The large-scale simulated dataset (11M+ events) with realistic Geant4/sPHENIX simulation and three downstream physics tasks is a valuable community resource.
The hierarchical raster scan serialization and k-next-nearest-neighbor objective are novel, physics-aware designs tailored to sparse 3D detector data.
The study demonstrates neural scaling behavior across model size, dataset size, and compute, a useful first for this domain.

Frozen pretrained features paired with lightweight adapters outperform adapted GNN and point-cloud baselines on track finding, particle identification, and noise tagging, with especially strong gains in low-label regimes.
Representation analyses (PCA/t-SNE) provide qualitative evidence that a single linear projection can specialize the learned embeddings to downstream tasks.
Weaknesses: Major numerical inconsistencies exist between the main table and appendix tables: for FM4NPP(m6), PID accuracy is reported as 0.9039 in Table 2 but 0.8547 in Appendix Table 4, and noise-tagging accuracy is 0.9713 vs 0.9662, with no explanation; this undermines confidence in the reported results.
No error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-seed results are provided for any downstream metric, so statistical significance of the claimed improvements is unclear.

The pretraining objective and serialization strategy are not ablated; sensitivity to the choice of k, binning granularity, alternative serializations (e.g., Hilbert curve), or alternative objectives (e.g., masked autoencoding) is unknown.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair: Exa.TrkX and EggNet were adapted with reduced features and manually chosen thresholds, OneFormer3D was used with default S3DIS hyperparameters, and no tuning-budget equivalence is established.

The claim that representations are task-agnostic and can be specialized via a 'single linear mapping' is overstated: downstream adapters include transformer layers, and only qualitative visualizations support this claim.

All experiments are on simulated p+p collisions at sPHENIX; no validation on real data, heavy-ion collisions, or other detector geometries is performed, so the 'foundation model' generalization claim is not fully supported.
The release of dataset, code, and pretrained checkpoints is not specified (no URL, license, or instructions), hindering reproducibility.
Questions: Which set of results is correct for FM4NPP(m6) on PID and noise tagging—Table 2 or Appendix Tables 3-4? Why do they differ?
Are all target neighbors in the k-next-nearest-neighbor objective strictly future tokens in the serialized sequence? If not, what prevents information leakage that could inflate performance?
What are the exact train/validation/test splits for each downstream task, and are pretraining and downstream evaluation events disjoint?

Were ablations performed on serialization choices (e.g., random, Hilbert, radial versus hierarchical raster scan) and on the value of k in the pretraining objective? What were the quantitative results?
Can you provide linear-probe accuracy or similar quantitative evidence for linear separability of frozen features on all three tasks, not just PCA/t-SNE?
How were the baseline models tuned, and were hyperparameters optimized with a comparable compute budget to the FM adapters?
What are the fitted scaling-law exponents and confidence intervals in Figure 5, and was the data-scaling curve verified for multiple model sizes?
What is the performance of the official sPHENIX pipeline on the full track sample, rather than only high-pT, long tracks with more than 20 hits?
Will the dataset, code, and trained models be publicly released, and under what license?
Limitations: The model is evaluated only on simulated p+p collisions at 200 GeV; transfer to real detector data, heavy-ion collisions, or other detector geometries is untested and likely requires redesign.
Only TPC spacepoints are used; calorimeter and silicon tracker information is excluded, limiting the scope of the foundation model.
The pretraining objective may suffer from information leakage due to non-strict radial ordering, which could inflate downstream performance.
No statistical uncertainties or seed variability are reported, so observed differences may not be reliable.
The largest model requires substantial compute (64 H100 GPUs for 72 hours), which may limit reproducibility.
The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section and does not discuss computational cost in FLOPs or energy consumption.
Downstream tasks are all point-level segmentation; other potentially relevant tasks such as regression, generation, or anomaly detection are not explored.
